slides.title: Recall five terms from Meeting A
rows: a quantity you are free to choose
x1 = solar m2, x2 = green roof m2
the one number you maximize or minimize
hard limits the design must satisfy
every (x1, x2) satisfying all constraints at once
c, A_ub, b_ub, bounds -> res.x, res.fun
slides.callout: Every term above appears at least once in today's script.
slides.teaching: Ask students to find each term already printed in their handout before running cell [1].

slides.title: Read the call before you run it
slides.teaching: Point at each chip in order before running cell [1] — this is the exact same four-array pattern every linprog call in today's script reuses. Name linprog itself as scipy's exact linear-program solver (already defined in the vocabulary table, previous slide).

slides.title: Binding vs. slack constraint
slides.definition: A constraint is BINDING when the optimum uses it up exactly (used = limit). A constraint is SLACK when the optimum satisfies it with room to spare. res.success is True either way — only hand-verification tells you which is which.

example.head: Radley Hall's roof (cells [2]-[4], next)
example.body: Area (200 m2) and budget ($50,000) both bind exactly at the optimum. The 120 m2 solar structural cap does not — only 80 m2 is used, 40 m2 of slack remains.

slides.note: res.success does not tell you which constraints bind — only Studio 2's hand-verification does.
slides.teaching: Preview that today's core exercise (Studio 2) is exactly this check, done by hand on Radley Hall's real numbers.

slides.title: Today's pipeline is four ordered steps

steps.label: FORMULATE
steps.head: Name the pieces
steps.body: Design variables, objective, constraints, and bounds — in words first, on paper.

steps.label: STANDARD FORM
steps.head: Translate to arrays
steps.body: c, A_ub, b_ub, bounds — the exact shape linprog expects.

steps.label: SOLVE + VERIFY
steps.head: Run, then hand-check
steps.body: linprog returns res.x; you confirm every constraint by hand before trusting it.

steps.label: TRANSFER
steps.head: Your own problem
steps.body: Repeat the same four steps on your own Project 2 linear sub-problem.

slides.teaching: This slide is the map of the whole studio — point back to it before each new cell.

slides.title: Predict before cell [1] runs
slides.code:
c = [-60, -25]
A_ub = [[1, 1], [400, 150]]
b_ub = [200, 50000]
bounds = [(0, 120), (0, None)]

res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
              bounds=bounds)
print(res.x, -res.fun)
slides.question: Which (x1, x2) allocation maximizes annual benefit here?
slides.why: res.x = [80, 120], -res.fun = 7800.0. (120,0) is tempting — solar earns more per m2 — but leaves 80 m2 of roof unused.
slides.teaching: Do not reveal the answer until cell [1] actually runs — most students pick (120,0) because solar's per-m2 return is higher.

slides.title: [1] Set up Radley Hall's roof in standard form, and solve
slides.code:
from scipy.optimize import linprog

c = [-60, -25]
A_ub = [[1, 1], [400, 150]]
b_ub = [200, 50000]
bounds = [(0, 120), (0, None)]
res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
              bounds=bounds, method='highs')
print(res.x)
print(res.fun)
print(res.success)
slides.explainHead: Read the raw solver output first
slides.explainBody: res.fun is -7800.0, not 7800.0 — it is the minimized NEGATIVE benefit, since linprog only minimizes. res.success is True: HiGHS found a feasible optimum, not that your formulation is correct — that is what hand-verification checks next. (Same c, A_ub, b_ub, bounds as the anatomy slide — area binds row 1, budget binds row 2.)
slides.teaching: Ask students to predict res.x from memory (Meeting A's answer) before running — by now they should say [80, 120] without checking.

slides.title: Studio 1: read the raw solver output correctly
slides.prompt: res.fun printed -7800.0, not 7800.0 — and res.success printed True.
steps: State in one sentence why res.fun is negative here.
Compute the real annual benefit by negating it yourself.
Confirm res.success is True before doing anything else.
Name what res.success being True does NOT prove.
slides.teaching: Expected answer to the last step: for this feasible bounded LP, the successful solver status supports a globally optimal solution to solver tolerances for whatever model was actually typed in — not that the typed-in formulation itself is correct. The AI-audit cell later makes this concrete.

slides.title: Predict before cells [2]-[3] run
slides.code:
x1, x2 = res.x        # 80.0, 120.0
area_used = x1 + x2
budget_used = 400*x1 + 150*x2
# structural cap: x1 <= 120
slides.question: Which constraint(s) bind exactly at (80, 120)?
options: Both the area limit and the budget cap
slides.why: area_used = 200.0 and budget_used = 50000.0 — both bind exactly. The structural cap has slack: only 80 of 120 m2 of solar is used.
slides.teaching: This is the exact question Studio 2 requires students to answer by hand next — do not reveal it until both cells run.

slides.title: [2] Hand-verify constraint 1: the area limit
slides.code:
x1, x2 = res.x
area_used = x1 + x2
print('area used:', area_used, '<= 200 ?', area_used <= 200)
slides.explainBody: 200.0 does not merely satisfy x1 + x2 <= 200 — it hits the limit EXACTLY. Every m2 of the 200 m2 roof is used; the area constraint binds.
slides.teaching: Have students compute 80 + 120 on paper before the cell runs — this is half of the studio's required core exercise.

slides.title: [3] Hand-verify constraint 2: the budget cap
slides.code:
budget_used = 400 * x1 + 150 * x2
print('budget used:', budget_used, '<= 50000 ?', budget_used <= 50000)
slides.explainHead: Both constraints bind, not by coincidence
slides.explainBody: $50,000.00 exactly — every dollar of the approved budget is spent. Two constraints, both binding exactly, is exactly what a corner-vertex solution (recall Meeting A) looks like in practice.
slides.teaching: Have students compute 400*80 + 150*120 on paper before the cell runs — the other half of the required core exercise.

slides.title: [4] Turn both hand-checks into real assertions
slides.code:
import numpy as np

assert np.isclose(area_used, 200.0, atol=1e-7)
assert np.isclose(budget_used, 50000.0, atol=1e-5)
print('Both constraints bind within tolerance.')
slides.explainBody: Optimization results are floating-point values. np.isclose makes the intended tolerance explicit, so harmless roundoff does not fail the script while a meaningful violation still does.
slides.teaching: Contrast with just trusting res.success — assert checks the ANSWER against the real-world limits, not just that the solver ran without error.

slides.title: Studio 2: hand-verify both binding constraints yourself
slides.prompt: Before trusting res.x = [80, 120], check it by hand — the studio's required core exercise.
steps: Compute 80 + 120 on paper — does it equal the 200 m2 roof limit?
Compute 400*80 + 150*120 on paper — does it equal the $50,000 budget?
State which TWO constraints bind, and which one (the structural cap) does not.
Explain in one sentence why 'the solver said success' is not enough on its own.
slides.teaching: This is the studio's required core exercise, named explicitly in the course plan. Every student must produce both hand-computations on paper, not just read the assert output.

slides.title: [5] Compare to the two 'obvious' strategies
slides.code:
benefit_allsolar = 60*120 + 25*0
benefit_allgreen = 60*0 + 25*200
benefit_opt = 60*x1 + 25*x2
print('all-solar:', benefit_allsolar)
print('all-green:', benefit_allgreen)
print('optimal:', benefit_opt)
slides.explainHead: Formulating beats guessing, by real dollars
slides.explainBody: All-solar (capped at 120 m2, 80 m2 unused) earns $7,200/yr. All-green earns $5,000/yr. The formulated-and-solved mix earns $7,800/yr — $600 to $2,800/yr more than either 'obvious' pure strategy, every year the roof stands.
slides.teaching: Ask which strategy students would have picked before this course — most say all-solar, since it has the higher per-m2 return.

slides.title: Same three numbers, now visible
slides.chartTitle: Radley Hall roof: annual benefit by strategy
slides.explainBody: Neither pure bar is tallest. This is the shape of comparison figure Project 2 Part II's rubric line expects: your own optimized result plotted against a naive baseline, not just reported as a number.
slides.teaching: Ask what a reader would wrongly assume about 'more solar is always better' if only the all-solar and all-green bars were shown, with the optimal bar left out.

slides.title: Studio 3: defend the optimal strategy in one sentence
slides.prompt: A colleague asks why you didn't just install solar everywhere possible.
steps: State solar's per-m2 benefit ($60) vs. green roof's ($25).
Explain why per-m2 return alone cannot decide a budget- and area-constrained problem.
Name the exact dollar gap between optimal and each naive strategy.
Write the one-sentence defense you would give the colleague.
slides.teaching: Expected defense: solar earns more per m2, but its install cost ($400/m2) also eats the budget faster — spending the whole budget on solar leaves 80 m2 of roof and cheaper green-roof benefit unused.

slides.title: Common linprog formulation errors
rows: Forgot to negate c when maximizing
Compare res.fun's sign to a hand guess
Solves a different region, no error
Ask whether the reported point is plausible
Print bounds; read each pair as (min, max)
A_ub row mixing per-m2 and total cost
Exact answer to the WRONG problem
slides.callout: The same failure mode as cell [6]'s AI-audit, next: success == True has never once meant 'correct.'
slides.teaching: Widen the lesson beyond the one bug in cell [6] — these four are the errors most often seen in AI-drafted formulations across student Project 2 drafts.

slides.title: Predict before cell [6] runs
slides.code:
# an AI assistant's suggested setup
c_ai = [60, 25]     # 'maximize benefit'
res_ai = linprog(c_ai, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
                  bounds=bounds)
slides.question: c_ai = [60, 25] replaces c = [-60, -25]. What happens?
options: res_ai.x = [0, 0], res_ai.fun = 0.0, and res_ai.success is still True
res_ai.success becomes False, flagging the mistake
slides.why: linprog always minimizes. c_ai=[60,25] asks it to minimize benefit, so the answer is 'build nothing': [0, 0], success still True.
slides.teaching: Do not reveal the fix yet — require students to name the defect from this prediction alone before cell [6] runs.

slides.title: [6] AI-audit: a plausible but wrong formulation
slides.code:
# an AI assistant's suggested setup for the SAME roof problem
c_ai = [60, 25]     # 'maximize benefit'
res_ai = linprog(c_ai, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
                  bounds=bounds, method='highs')
print(res_ai.x, res_ai.fun)
slides.explainHead: success is True here too — and still wrong
slides.explainBody: res_ai.success would still print True: the solver correctly minimized 60x1+25x2, exactly as typed. But 'maximize benefit' needs the NEGATED coefficients (c = [-60, -25], cell [1]) — forgetting the negation quietly turns the problem into 'minimize benefit,' whose answer is do nothing at all.
slides.teaching: Give students this exact code and output. Require them to name the defect before showing the fix — do not reveal the corrected c_ai yet.

slides.title: Studio 4: diagnose and repair the AI-drafted formulation
slides.prompt: res_ai.x = [0, 0] with res_ai.success = True — no error was ever raised.
steps: Name exactly which line contains the defect.
Explain why linprog accepted it without any error message.
Rewrite c_ai correctly and re-run.
Confirm the repaired version reproduces [80, 120] and 7800.0.
slides.teaching: Require students to state the general rule, not just this one instance: linprog ALWAYS minimizes; a maximize objective must be negated before it is handed to c.

slides.title: Predict before cell [7] runs
slides.code:
# transfer check: the board approves only $40,000
b_ub_new = [200, 40000]
res_new = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub_new,
                   bounds=bounds)
slides.question: Budget drops to $40,000 — predict (x1, x2).
slides.why: res_new.x = [40, 160], -res_new.fun = 6400.0. Solar's $400/m2 install eats the smaller budget faster, so the mix shifts to green roof.
slides.teaching: Point out the budget WAS binding at $50,000 (cell [3]) — so it cannot possibly stay unchanged once the budget shrinks. Some students still guess (80,120) out of habit.

slides.title: [7] Self-check: a smaller approved budget
slides.code:
# transfer check: the board approves only $40,000 this year
b_ub_new = [200, 40000]
res_new = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub_new,
                   bounds=bounds, method='highs')
print(res_new.x, -res_new.fun)
slides.explainHead: Same formula, a genuinely different input
slides.explainBody: Only b_ub's second entry changed — $40,000 instead of $50,000 — and the optimal mix shifted to 40 m2 solar, 160 m2 green roof, $6,400/yr. Both constraints still bind exactly: 40+160=200 and 400*40+150*160=40,000.
slides.teaching: This is the exact 'different input' the course's transfer safeguard requires — name it as such to students.

slides.title: A smaller budget shifts the split, not just the total
slides.chartTitle: Optimal allocation at two approved budgets
slides.explainBody: At $40,000 the optimum is 40 m2 solar / 160 m2 green roof ($6,400/yr); at $50,000 it is 80/120 ($7,800/yr). Both scenarios still use every m2 of roof and every dollar of budget — only the SPLIT changes, not which two constraints bind.
slides.teaching: Tie this directly to Studio 5's required transfer asserts, next — the pattern (both area and budget bind) is what those asserts actually check on the new numbers.

slides.title: Studio 5: write your own required transfer assertions
slides.prompt: Turn the check above into 2-4 self-written assert statements — this week's required transfer safeguard.
steps: Assert res_new.x[0] + res_new.x[1] == 200.
Assert 400*res_new.x[0] + 150*res_new.x[1] == 40000.
Assert round(-res_new.fun, 2) == 6400.0.
Run from a restarted kernel and confirm silent success.
slides.teaching: Required, graded transfer-safeguard element — a different budget number than the one worked through live, with the student's own asserts, not optional polish.

slides.title: [8] Package formulate, solve, and verify as one function
slides.code:
def solve_roof_allocation(area_limit_m2: float,
                          budget_usd: float) -> dict:
    """Solve one roof scenario; check both limits."""
    c = [-60, -25]  # maximize -> minimize -60x1-25x2
    A_ub = [[1, 1], [400, 150]]  # area row, cost row
    b_ub = [area_limit_m2, budget_usd]
    bounds = [(0, 120), (0, None)]  # solar cap 120
    res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub,
                  bounds=bounds, method='highs')
    x1, x2 = res.x
    area_used = x1 + x2
    cost_used = 400 * x1 + 150 * x2
slides.explainHead: The same four arrays, written once
slides.explainBody: Cells [1] and [7] typed the same formulation twice, changing only b_ub. A function makes that honest: area_limit_m2 and budget_usd become parameters because they are what actually changes, while the $400/$150 install costs, the $60/$25 benefits, and the 120 m2 structural cap stay fixed inside. The docstring and type hints are the Week 4 convention. area_used and cost_used are the same hand-checks from cells [2]-[3], now recomputed on every call.
slides.teaching: Put cell [1] and cell [7] side by side and ask what actually differs — only b_ub's second entry. That is exactly the signal a parameter belongs there. Then ask why the 120 m2 structural cap is NOT a parameter: nothing in this studio ever changes it.

slides.title: ...continued: [9] return the checks, then reuse on 3 budgets
slides.explainHead: One function, three scenarios, zero retyping
slides.explainBody: The dict returns the answer AND its proof together, so nothing can read solar_m2 without also seeing area_binds. The assert then turns Studio 2's one-time hand-check into a permanent, automatic check that runs on every scenario: at $50,000 the split is 80/120 ($7,800/yr), at $45,000 it is 60/140 ($7,100/yr), and at $40,000 it is 40/160 ($6,400/yr) — each of them spending all 200 m2 and every approved dollar.
slides.teaching: Ask what it takes to test a fourth budget: one more number in the list on the for line. Note the assert sits INSIDE the loop, so a scenario that ever stopped binding would halt the script on that scenario and name it. Verified against real scipy 1.17.1.

slides.title: Today's milestone, stated plainly

left.head: What's required
left.body: Formulate the linear sub-component of YOUR OWN Project 2 problem — or a simplified linear relaxation of it, if your real problem is not naturally linear — naming design variables, objective, constraints, and bounds, then solve it with linprog.

right.head: Why this counts as the milestone
right.body: This studio task IS Project 2's topic/dataset/pairing proposal AND its linear-formulation-family justification, per the course's assignment policy — nothing separate to additionally produce.

slides.teaching: State plainly that a simplified linear relaxation is fully acceptable and expected if a student's real problem is not naturally linear — the point is demonstrating the formulate-solve-verify skill, not forcing every real problem into a linear shape.

slides.title: Predict before cell [10] runs
slides.question: Same pattern, a different problem: which constraint(s) bind?
options: Both the glazing-area limit and the budget cap
slides.why: res_w.x = [100, 50]: area 100+50 = 150 m2 binds; budget 250*100+500*50 = $50,000 binds. The triple-pane cap has slack (50 of 80).
slides.teaching: A genuinely different problem (window retrofit, not the roof) — the pattern of two constraints binding and one slack repeats, which is the actual lesson, not the specific numbers.

slides.title: [10] One illustrative example, before you build your own
slides.code:
# ILLUSTRATIVE second problem - a window-retrofit budget (NOT your own
# Project 2 problem; replace every line with YOUR real variables)
c_w = [-18, -30]
A_ub_w = [[1, 1], [250, 500]]
b_ub_w = [150, 50000]
bounds_w = [(0, None), (0, 80)]
res_w = linprog(c_w, A_ub=A_ub_w, b_ub=b_ub_w,
                 bounds=bounds_w, method='highs')
print(res_w.x, -res_w.fun)
slides.explainHead: A template to adapt, not to copy
slides.explainBody: A different fictional problem (standard vs. triple-pane window retrofit, $250/$500 per m2 install, $18/$30 per m2/yr savings, 150 m2 total glazing, $50,000 budget, triple-pane supply capped at 80 m2) — shown only so the same four-array pattern (c, A_ub, b_ub, bounds) is visible once more before you write your own. Here the glazing-area limit binds (150 m2 used) and the budget binds ($50,000 used), while the triple-pane supply cap (80 m2) has slack at 50 m2 used — not every constraint has to bind.
slides.teaching: Point out this is a genuinely different problem, not a relabeled roof — the lesson is the PATTERN (name variables, write objective, write constraints as A_ub rows, set bounds, solve, verify), not this specific numbers.

slides.title: Studio 6: formulate and solve your own Project 2 sub-problem
slides.prompt: Using the exact same four steps as Radley Hall's roof, formulate your own problem's linear sub-component.
steps: Name your design variables, with units.
Write your objective function, stating whether you are maximizing or minimizing.
Write every constraint as an A_ub/b_ub row, plus any bounds.
Solve with linprog and hand-verify every constraint, exactly like Studio 2.
slides.teaching: This IS the graded weekly assignment and the Project 2 milestone — a simplified linear relaxation is fully acceptable if a student's real problem is not naturally linear, per course policy.

slides.title: Preview: next week, no exact guarantee
slides.statement: Week 11's objective curves — the feasible-region guarantee disappears, and minimize must search from a starting guess.
slides.supporting: Today's linprog returned a globally optimal LP solution to solver tolerances for this feasible bounded model, with no starting guess. Next week, the SAME kind of decision (design variables, an objective, bounds) is solved by a genuinely different method — watch for what changes and what does not.

slides.title: Formulate, solve, verify — in that order, every time
takeaways: linprog needs the correct sign on c — forgetting to negate a maximize objective silently returns 'do nothing,' with res.success still True.
res.success == True proves the solver found an optimum of what you typed — never skip hand-verifying every constraint yourself.
Radley Hall's roof rewards a mixed strategy ($7,800/yr) over either 'obvious' pure one ($7,200 or $5,000/yr) — formulating beats guessing.
Today's studio — formulate, solve, and verify your own Project 2 linear sub-problem — IS this week's milestone, not an additional task.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students state, in one sentence, which optimization family (linear, gradient-based, or heuristic) their own Project 2 sub-problem uses today, and why.
